subject: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test

messages.author: 39f1ac78bd3926ba
messages.subject: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
parts:
Dear all,

I am currently working on examining longitudinal measurement invariance in a 9-wave annual dataset for a 3-item measure of self-esteem. In one analysis, I wrote the script (model_1), shown below, using the cfa() function. I fit this to a wide version of my dataset (i.e., one row per participant with the assessments per wave as different variables). I found that the model fit for the configural model was CFI = .849, RMSEA = .059, and very similarly for the weak model, CFI = .849, RMSEA = .059.

However, I found a technical paper in which invariance was tested for the same dataset using the now-deprecated measurementInvariance() function (model_2), shown below. In this paper, a long version of the dataset was used (i.e., one row per assessment wave). They reported different fit statistics, so that for the configural model, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000, and for the weak model, CFI = .995, RMSEA = .054.

To better understand where the difference in fit came from, I inspected the code behind the measurementInvariance() function, which I then tested in the long dataset with the cfa() subcommand “group=“wave” (model_3), shown below. This model yielded the same fit statistics as the model I fit with the measurementInvariance() command. I then tried to write out the model fully in longhand (i.e., without using the “group =” subcommand in the cfa() function; see model_4). However, if I fit this model to the wide dataset I am unable to replicate the statistics of model 2 and 3, and instead get a model fit of CFI = .616, RMSEA = .105.

My question now is why model 4 does not yield the same estimates as models 2 and 3 do. Is there a mistake in my model specification? Or is there a logical reason for why the estimates differ that I’m missing?

Many thanks in advance for your help.

Best,
Elisabeth de Moor

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
parts:
Analyzing longitudinal data as multigroup data ignores the dependence among observations.  The dependence is represented in the covariances among variables across occasions in a longitudinal model.  You are not fitting the same model to the same data (i.e., 324 observed between-time covariances between 3 variables across 9 occasions disappear), and you should not treat occasions as independent groups.

FYI, there is a longInvariance() function (also deprecated) that would be more appropriate for your situation.  There is also a measEq.syntax() function that is much more pedagogically useful, as the whole point is that it writes syntax you can inspect.  The first help-page example has a longitudinal (2-occasion) model, as well as 2 groups, but you can ignore the group arguments and just adapt it to your 9-occasion example.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts:
Hi Patrick and Terrence,

Thank you for thinking along with me on this issue!

It is good to hear that me not being able to replicate the multigroup model fit statistics in the longhand model is to be expected. I did consider the difference between the longitudinal versus multigroup measurement invariance models in their treatment of covariances between the latent constructs across waves/groups, but did not realize fully the extent of this difference (324 is a lot!). 

I further thank you for the suggestions of other functions to use for this purpose. The invariance tests using the waves as groups were conducted in a previous study rather than my own, but it is good to know functions like this also exist to examine longitudinal measurement invariance. I particularly like the measEq.syntax() suggestion, because it allows inspection of the fitted model. This in particular was one of the difficulties I faced in comparing the findings from the measurementInvariance() function used in the prior study to my own longhand syntax.

Best,
Elisabeth
